name: Granian
workload: ASGI HTTP GET request returning a 10KB static plain-text response, benchmarked with `oha` at concurrency 128 for 10s (after a primer/warmup run), single worker/thread, HTTP/1.1; all async servers including the baseline use uvloop as the asyncio event loop.
claimed_speedup: 125,539 RPS (Granian ASGI) vs 14,501 RPS (Uvicorn H11 on uvloop) = ~8.66x; vs 51,051 RPS (Uvicorn Httptools on uvloop) = ~2.46x (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: Rust, built via `maturin build --release --features jemalloc` (see benchmarks/runbench.sh)
tradeoffs: Rust/PyO3 build dependency (maturin); single benchmark run, not averaged over repeated trials; desktop CPU rather than a controlled cloud instance
caveats: First-party benchmark (project's own repo) but the harness (benchmarks.py, runbench.sh, envs/) and build flags are public and reproducible, and hardware/CPU model are stated, so it clears the Tier A bar.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "fastest http server" -> README links to benchmarks/vs.md

name: hyper
workload: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks community shootout: minimal plaintext HTTP response benchmarked with wrk at concurrency levels 64/256/512 across 380+ frameworks.
claimed_speedup: 166,617 req/s (hyper) vs 163,415 req/s (actix v4.8) at concurrency 512 = ~1.02x (derived from page data)
hardware: 16 CPUs, host CPU labeled 'M1 Eight-Core Processor' in data.json hardware field, Linux 7.2.6-200.fc44.x86_64, run dated 2026-09-24
stars_or_usage: 16.3k stars; underlies axum, warp, and much of the Rust HTTP ecosystem
tradeoffs: hyper is a low-level HTTP library, not a full framework like actix-web, so the raw-hyper shootout entry has less framework overhead by construction (apples-to-oranges)
caveats: Margin is only ~2%, within noise for a single-run community wrk shootout; per-framework Dockerfile build flags were not individually inspected, so compiler/flags are unconfirmed (caps tier at B, not A).
found_via: GitHub: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks data.json, rust-language ranking sorted by total_requests_per_s

name: Ultimate Express
workload: wrk load test (-d 60 -t 1 -c 200) across 8 route/middleware scenarios (simple routing, many routes, nested routers, static files, EJS templates, body parsing, compression), Express 4 vs Ultimate Express (uWebSockets.js-based drop-in replacement), Node.js 20.17.0.
claimed_speedup: 4.87x-11.78x depending on scenario, e.g. 75.14k req/s vs 11.16k req/s on simple routing (6.73x); 54.57k vs 4.63k req/s on many-routes (11.78x)
tradeoffs: Built on uWebSockets.js (native C++ core via N-API); not a 100% Express match (documented differences: case-sensitive routing by default, opt-in body parsing, different HTTPS setup)
caveats: Benchmark code is public (/benchmark directory) and hardware + Node version + wrk params are stated, but it is a single-machine, single-run first-party measurement with no repeated-trial averaging shown. Baseline (Express.js) is not one of the 5 named category baselines; recorded honestly with baseline_in_list=false.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "fastest http server"

name: Qbix Server (PHP webserver)
workload: PHP request handling under a simulated 50ms I/O wait, comparing php-fpm's 4 persistent workers vs Qbix Server's 40 COW-forked persistent workers within the same fixed 200MB memory budget; single-core container, PHP 8.3.6, Ubuntu 24, benchmarked with `ab`.
claimed_speedup: 1,060 req/s (Qbix, 40 workers) vs 78 req/s (php-fpm, 4 workers) at the same 200MB memory budget = ~13.6x (doc states '14x') (derived from page data)
hardware: single-core container, Ubuntu 24, PHP 8.3.6; no CPU model stated
tradeoffs: Relies on pcntl_fork() (Unix/Linux only, no Windows); the memory/worker-count advantage under I/O-bound load is the whole story, not raw per-request latency; on CPU-bound work it loses to Swoole (439 vs 483 req/s) and roughly ties php-fpm.
caveats: In the SAME benchmark document, nginx directly beats Qbix on static file serving (50,742 req/s vs Qbix's 18,311 req/s), so the project's README tagline of beating nginx is not supported for that workload; the substantiated win is specifically against php-fpm's worker-count ceiling under I/O-bound load. No CPU model is stated ('single-core container'), which caps this at Tier C rather than A/B.
found_via: HN Algolia search "faster than nginx" -> Qbix/webserver README/docs
